cards.note: Roofs featuring an arrow-shaped extension protruding upwards are common in the eastern half of Java.

Various styles of thick, baroque-style ornately-decorated rooftops can be found in East Java.

Ornate rooftops featuring these semicircular openings, usually disconnected at the bottom, can be found in western East Java.

Ornate rooftops featuring these tripoint designs are further localised within western East Java. They often, but not always, also feature the semicircular openings noted above.

Dhurung Bawean is a traditional architectural structure on the Indonesian island of Bawean, which serves as a lumbung (storehouse) for harvests and as an outdoor gathering place for social activities and guests. It is characterised by an unusually large roof structure supported by wooden pillars.

cards.a: Java - Bawean Island Red Ridge Tiles
cards.note: Roofs similar to those found on Bangka Island are very common. These typically consist of fibre cement sheets and** reddish tiles lining the edges**. The second type of roof that is also frequently found is the fully tiled Javanese roof.
In a similar area, you will find roof ridges spanned by perforated bricks.

Candi Bentar or “split gates” appear like a single structure split into two and are vestiges of Hinduism on Java. The sides facing each other are plain while the outsides may be highly ornate. They may be red brick or painted. They can be found at historic sites across Java but are most common in East Java.

Thin metal sheets with curled ends spanning the roof ridges are a common sight across most of eastern Central Java. They also frequently feature a central ornament displaying the year of construction.

The simplest of the three roof types is the Double-Pitched-Roof. It is characterised by a multi-angled roof structure, but with only two different roof angles. Each roof surface is parallel to the long side of the house.

Many Javanese roofs feature narrow, vertical wooden attachments at or below the end of the roof ridge. They often appear as an upward or downward pointed arrow, but can feature a wide range of designs (e.g., heart, anchor, fork). Regardless of shape, these attachments are found commonly in East Java and also appear routinely in Central Java and Yogyakarta. Note that similar designs can sometimes be found outside Java.
Flexible roof sheets are very common around Pulosari and Watoekoempoel in western Central Java, as well as in the villages south of Mount Lawu in the far eastern part of the province.

The area around Mount Bromo, especially along its northern face surrounding Wonokitri, is home to the Tenggerese - the last Hindu-majority people in Java.

The region features many Hindu design elements, the most distinct being these small shrines (Pelinggih) which are often found at intersections or in front of homes.

The region can be differentiated from Bali by the very mountainous setting with lots of mountain casuarina (she-oak) trees.
A lot of industrial parks can be found near the outskirts of Jakarta Metropolitan Area.
Jakarta has many narrow alleys where pedestrians, motorcycles and cars travel. Sometimes you can see skyscrapers in the distance.
Small tooth-like embellishments and filigree motifs along the ridge and edges of the roof are common in the regencies of Jepara, Kudus and Pati. Rare examples also exist further south.
Joglo houses feature a steep ‘hat’ shaped roof surrounded by large flaps on all four sides.

Rembang Regency is home to a unique traditional house known as the Joglo Bocokan. It is characterised by a Joglo base with gables on the sides, as opposed to slopes. A small transverse roof may or may not be present inside the gable.
South-west of Mount Lawu, located in eastern Central Java, metal triangles with jagged edges can be seen adorning the end of roof ridges on corrugated metal rooftops.
In the southeastern mountainous part of Banten, traditional Sundanese rice barns known as Leuit are still common.
Limasan roofs also have a multi-angled roof structure, but unlike Joglo roofs, they are shallower and the flap is only present on two sides.

Limestone bricks are common in northern East Java, including Madura Island, reflecting the limestone geology of the area. The bricks are put together with thick grey mortar, creating a striking visual distinction.
**Roof ridges made out of smooth cement **are quite common on Madura, especially on Limasan-style roofs. Some roofs on Madura feature these stubby concrete spikes on each end of the rooftop.

cards.a: Java - Madura Limestone Bricks Red Mortar
cards.note: In the eastern part of Madura Island, houses feature walls made of white bricks and thick red mortar instead of grey, reflecting the local geology.
Small stilt houses with Limasan roofs are often found near traditional Madurese settlements. These stilts sometimes rest on stone foundations.

Traditional Madurese settlements, called Tanèyan Lanjhang, consist of two or more buildings arranged around a rectangular courtyard. The main building often joins two or more identical units together.
Metal eaves installed along the edges of the roof are highly localised to the northeastern part of Central Java. Metal eaves most commonly come in the colours blue, green, or red.

Although Java is well-known for its tiled roofs, communities featuring heavy or predominant use of metal roofs can be found in a number of mountainous and coastal areas on Java. Notable examples include the areas surrounding Mount Slamet (Central Java) and Mount Bromo (East Java).

Villages located along the southern coastal plain of Central Java, particularly in the regions stretching west of Yogyakarta, are characterised by an organised layout of small rectangular properties framed by short, neatly-trimmed hedges. These settlements mostly follow a strict grid-like pattern with a noticeable absence of winding roads.
Roads flanked by these standalone decorative entrance pillars are common in East Java, eastern Central Java, and Yogyakarta. These may mark the entrance to a property or village.
Highly decorated metal or concrete triangles are seen spanning the entire ridges of roofs in Pati and Rembang regencies.

Conversely, roof ridge ends with a roughly octagonal shape are common in East Java, but are very rare on the rest of the island. Note that the diagonal sides are usually curved inward, somewhat resembling a plus (“+”) shape.

The ends of roof ridges in Java have various shapes that can be helpful for narrowing down your location on the island. Roof ridge ends in a pentagonal shape are common in Banten, West Java and Central Java, but are quite rare in East Java.

In East Java, ridge ends often stick out a small distance past the end of the roof itself. This can be very subtle, but in the right lighting it can sometimes be identified by the presence of a small shadow underneath the ridge end.

Diverse roof ornaments are a common sight throughout East Java as well as eastern Central Java. These roof ornaments mostly feature winged or curled shapes and animal motifs, located at the ends and peaks of roof ridges.
Ridges featuring multiple stacked roof tiles are particularly common in the eastern part of Central Java. You will also spot this feature in some areas of East Java.
Roof tiles with this staggered, alternating pattern can be found throughout Java, but are most common in East Java and adjacent parts of Central Java.

Throughout Banten and the mountainous south of West Java, many houses rest on stone pedestals, leaving the natural ground beneath exposed. These stone bases provide a level foundation, compensating for the uneven terrain in rural areas.

Thatched roofs are a common sight throughout Banten, especially in rural regions. While they aren't unique to Banten and appear sporadically in other parts of Java, high concentrations are found only here and in a small section of West Java.
These distinctive Balinese-style roof ornaments, consisting of long flat wing shapes with curled ends can be found in the far eastern end of Java.
Around Mount Merbabu (just north of Yogyakarta) the Mount Merbabu zi8gzag wings occur. Small, wing-like structures, almost always in a zigzag pattern, adorn the ends of roof ridges.

In parts of South Kalimantan, you can see the traditional chieftains’ houses of the Banjar people. These are known as Rumah Bubungan Tinggi, meaning 'high peak' houses, due to their steep gable roofs. The whole house is built on top of high stilts.

In the coastal cities of West Kalimantan, especially Pontianak, you will occasionally see bright-yellow buildings and monuments. The colour dates back to the Pontianak Sultanate, where yellow signified Malay royalty, and the tradition has persisted locally.
Simple, elevated houses built on wooden stilts with Buginese roof features can be found along the north-east coast of Kalimantan.

Along the west coast of West Kalimantan, especially in the northwest and the city of Singkawang, you will notice a lot of Chinese architecture and inscriptions. As well as the distinctive paifang-style gates and klenteng (temples), there are many Chinese cemeteries with characteristic rounded, horseshoe-shaped tombs. Similar features appear across Indonesia wherever there are sizable Chinese communities, but West Kalimantan has the largest Chinese population in Indonesia.
The further north-east you go in Kalimantan, the more likely you are to find houses painted in bright colours.

The Dayak are the indigenous people of Borneo and generally inhabit more inland parts of the island. Malinau, Kutai Barat and Sintang regencies have the most prominent Dayak populations.

Dayak traditional art is extremely intricate and curvy and can be found painted on walls, fences, poles and other surfaces. Key motifs include the Aso (a mythical hybrid of a dog and dragon representing strength), the Hornbill (symbolising nobility and bravery), and an elongated hexagonal shield.
Rosette designs on gables are fairly common in West Kalimantan. They can be seen elsewhere in Indonesia too, but within Kalimantan, they are most likely to be seen in West Kalimantan.

In the south of South Kalimantan you will find many of the same features that are associated with Lampung, including Hindu religious structures, property entrance wing walls, and sticks used as bollards.
Banjarese houses in South Kalimantan have wide, horizontal boards spanning the top of the front of the houses. These boards can be wooden or metal.
Many modern houses in South Kalimantan incorporate elements of the traditional Banjarese traditional Gajah Manusu houses. In particular, they often feature its signature jerkinhead roof.
Within Kalimantan, Lampung-style tiled roofs are found in the provinces of Central, South and East Kalimantan.
Houses with long wooden walkways leading up to them from the road are more common towards North and East Kalimantan, but are found sporadically across all of Kalimantan.

Monumental Malay-style halls appear occasionally in West Kalimantan. Typical features include a broad central staircase, spacious verandas and numerous tall stilts. You will also find modern variants that keep only some elements, principally the grand, columned look.

The traditional longhouse is the most iconic architectural form of the Dayak people across Kalimantan and is the core of their communal and social life. These longhouses are more common inland and in northern parts of Kalimantan.

Houses in the south-east of Kalimantan sometimes feature a prominent set of uniform vertical panels that serve as the main front access to the house. The panels are framed in a distinct colour creating a striking facade.
Houses with traditional wooden shingles are present in Central, South and East Kalimantan.

These tall wooden towers are used for farming swallows’ nests, a Chinese delicacy. Concrete versions of the structure are common across Kalimantan; however, the wooden variant is mostly only present in the eastern half of Kalimantan.

At the northern tip of North Maluku, modern versions of the traditional Sasadu house with a highly recognisable metal roof construction can be found. The roof shape consists of a Bangla roof with a particularly protruding gable.
Traditional houses on Alor have a characteristic arrow-tip shape, are raised on stilts and feature thatched or sheet metal roofs.
Houses on Alor often have a lower section made of brick and an upper section made of woven bamboo matting.
Long rock walls are common on Alor. However unlike those on Rote, these walls are not made from limestone, so the stones are smoother, like large pebbles.
Windows with bamboo mesh coverings are also a distinctive feature of houses on Alor.

cards.a: Nusas - Alor, Lembata & Adonara Wide Spaced Fences
cards.note: Bamboo fences on Alor, Lembata and Adonara have noticeably large open spaces between both horizontal and vertical bamboo bars.

These beautifully carved split gates, known as Candi Bentar, are a quintessential element of Balinese Hindu architecture. On Bali, they are predominantly crafted from dark, volcanic basalt. While they typically mark property entrances, they occasionally appear on public roads as well.
A Penjor is an elaborately decorated, long bamboo pole that serves as an important ritual object in Balinese Hinduism.
In Bali, properties are typically enclosed by high stone walls, often adorned with basalt ornamentation.

Roof ornaments are a staple of Balinese architecture. Common features include crown-like decorations and wing-like finials at the roof ridge ends, often combined with a central element. These designs are also present in western Lombok and in neighbouring East Java, which have large Balinese populations
Western Flores is inhabited by the Manggarai people and their villages are usually centred around a traditional chieftain's house with a conical roof and a distinctive finial.

Roofs shaped like hats are common in central Flores in areas that are ethnically Ngada, Nage and Ende. There is a very high concentration in the ethnically Ngada area around Bajawa where the houses also have distinct ornaments on both ends of the top beam.

Inhabitants of Komodo Island are descendants of Bugis from Sulawesi and of former convicts who were abandoned on the island. Buginese architecture therefore dominates, with triangular gables and gable horns. Green and blue are the most common colours, and houses are often built on stilts. Property boundaries are sometimes marked with loose rocks.

This curved roof shape in Lombok is influenced by the traditional rice barns of the Sasak tribe. Whilst rice barns in their traditional form are rare, their influence can be seen in the shapes of houses, gates and shelters throughout Lombok.
Apart from ordinary Javanese tiles, roofs made of grey tiles are almost exclusive to Lombok. Another feature of Lombok architecture is the grey concrete block walls that surround properties.
Red brick houses are widespread on the Nusa islands of Sumbawa and Alor. They also occur on Lombok, Flores, Lembata and Adonara, but less frequently.
Fences made from palm stalks in a tight wicker-weave pattern are common on Rote.
On Rote, plots of land and fields are surrounded by distinctive long walls made from piled-up stones.
Houses made entirely of bamboo materials with sheet metal roofs are also frequently found on Sumba.
Graves on the predominantly Christian Sumba are often in the shape of a rectangular frustum with a flat table-like top.
The traditional houses of Sumba, known as Uma Mbatangu, feature soaring, high-pitched roofs that taper dramatically into a pointed apex, which is decorated on both sides with upright finials.
On the western tip of Sumba you can find these types of traditional houses with thatched roofs. The white brick houses typical of the Nusas are also found all over Sumba.

A good indicator for Sumbawa is tiled Buginese houses. These are recognisable by their tiled horizontal roof flap across the gable. The tiles are often the same style that is found on Java. This style of tile is not found on Sulawesi. These houses also typically lack balconies and are surrounded by fences.
On Sumbawa, you will find an unusually high number of sheet metal fences compared to the rest of Indonesia. Fences and gates made of bamboo are also common.

cards.a: Nusas - Sumbawa Tiled And Metall Roofs
cards.note: Sumbawa marks the boundary of the transition from tiled roofs to sheet metal roofs. While a mix of both can be found on the island’s west side, the east side is dominated by sheet metal roofing.

cards.a: Nusas - Timor & Rote Timber Frame Houses
cards.note: The most distinctive house types on Timor feature a boxy timber frame central section infilled with palm or bamboo. This type of house may also rarely be found on Rote.

Traditional bamboo houses with thatched roofs are found scattered across Timor. These houses sometimes have a circular shape. Modern versions with metal roofs can also be found. Unlike Manggarai chieftain houses, these often have a short ridge with two small horns along the top.
These pavilions on stilts with a pyramidal roof can be found throughout Lombok and Sumbawa.
White brick houses are widespread on the Nusa islands of Timor, Rote and Sumba while red brick houses are much less common.

The architecture of Selayar Island is characterised by the large number of Bugis-style houses. These sometimes have thatched gables. Modern houses typically have fibre cement roofs with sheet metal lining the edges.

Note: The elements mentioned are to be understood as a combination specific to Selayar Island. Individual elements, such as fiber cement roofs with metal lining, also occur elsewhere.
In addition to Sula fences, many bamboo fences can be found in the southern part of the South East Sulawesi.

In the southern part of South Sulawesi, including Selayar Island, you can sometimes find bamboo-lattice pavilions. These mark the entryway from the roadside to a household property and range from simple flat arches to small roofed pavilions.
Brick manufacturing is common across Peleng Island. White bricks and sometimes the sand needed for their production, can be seen stored along the narrow roads.

Bugis houses are typically elongated wooden stilt houses elevated well above the ground.

They are topped by a simple gabled roof. The front gable often features a distinctive finial. The houses also have a gable end formed from panels and with a distinctive shape. The number of overlapping panels indicates the social status of the owner.

Access to these houses is via a steep, usually single-flight staircase leading directly to a protruding open or semi-open veranda.

As well as the traditional Tongkonan houses with saddle-shaped roofs, the area around Tana Toraja contains houses influenced by both the local traditional architecture and Buginese architecture. These commonly feature multi-layered gable roofs with a slight bulge at the end.

This roof type can also be found in two other areas: one south of Lake Matano and another east of Lake Poso in Central Sulawesi.

Meanwhile, Buol Regency favours a green and yellow colour scheme. You will see these colours on political posters, official buildings, fences, and monuments. However, keep in mind that the majority of Sula fences here remain mostly blue and white, similar to those in Toli-Toli Regency.

Architecture in Central Sulawesi is defined by its simplicity. Throughout the province, simple wooden houses are very common, but the most widespread building material is unplastered grey brick, which is far more prevalent than red brick. It is common to see houses where the front facade has been painted while the sides remain exposed and unplastered.
Throughout Central Sulawesi, villages are characterised by neatly maintained, low-growing hedges that frequently feature blooming pink flowers.

Toli-Toli Regency is the home of the Dondo people. Their traditional dwellings are very simple, rustic-looking wooden houses built on stilts. These structures are typically longer than they are wide and are built from raw, untreated wood. They also feature gable roofs and simple wooden bridges leading to the entrance.

The old town area around the harbour of** Donggala** featured well-preserved Dutch colonial architecture. Most striking are the buildings with** rounded corners,** a design element rarely seen elsewhere in Indonesia.
Many villages in South East Sulawesi have grid-like layouts and well-maintained hedges, which are often strikingly long.
In the central southern part of South East Sulawesi, you can find a lot of Hindu-related architecture.

Cultural influences are also visible in the landscape; small Hindu gardens featuring statues are present throughout the province, with particular hotspots located on the Banggai Peninsula and along the coast south of Parigi.

Banua, the traditional houses of the Mamasa people in West Sulawesi, have distinctive roofs. These are arched with curves upwards at both ends. They are usually asymmetrical, with one of the ends taller than the other. Ordinary houses can also have an asymmetrical slight upward curve.

The houses of the Minahasa people are the most distinctive architectural feature of North Sulawesi, constructed entirely of light orange-brown wood and featuring a unique roof shape with triangular elements similar to stacked Bangla roofs. The classic Minahasa house is a two-storey building on stilts, although single-storey houses also exist.

cards.a: Sulawesi - Muna Buton Horizontally Painted Fences
cards.note: Sula fences painted red-and white horizontally, on the other hand, are common on Buton Island. These can also rarely be found on Muna Island.

On Muna Island and Buton Island, you can see houses built from vertical wooden planks painted in alternating colours. Unpainted houses built from vertical planks are also generally indicative of the area, but less reliable.

Many of the houses are built on stilts. Often there are support beams connecting the stilts to the main body of the house. Some houses also have foundations.

cards.a: Sulawesi - Muna Buton Lava Rock Walls
cards.note: Walls made of dark rough-textured lava rocks are common on Muna Island and Buton Island. You will also see lighter but similarly shaped rocks in walls on these islands.

cards.a: Sulawesi - Muna Buton Red White Walls
cards.note: A good identifying feature of Muna Island and Buton Island is white and red walls. The posts of the wall are often topped with a rounded finial in a shape reminiscent of the dome of a mosque.

cards.a: Sulawesi - Muna Buton Vertically Painted Fences
cards.note: Sula fences painted in alternating white and red sections are the most common type of fence on Muna Island. They can also sometimes be found along the west coast of Buton Island. Outside of these two islands, the fence variant may also occur.

cards.a: Sulawesi - North Maluku Canopies & Stone Foundations
cards.note: Houses in North Maluku often have large canopies and visible stone foundations. Note that most houses in the province are more recently-built, so exposed cinder blocks and shiny or coloured metal roofs are common.

cards.a: Sulawesi - North Maluku Low Concrete Walls
cards.note: Low concrete walls in various colours with vertical slots in the middle are very common in North Maluku. Sula fences can also occur, but less frequently.
In Polewali Mandar Regency, you can find Sula fences in an orange-blue colour combination.

cards.a: Sulawesi - Selayar Island Floral Window Motifs
cards.note: Windows of modern dwellings on Selayar Island sometimes feature colourful floral decorations.

cards.a: Sulawesi - Selayar Island Low Concrete Walls
cards.note: Sula fences and low concrete walls are common on Selayar Island. On the outskirts of the city of Bentang, you can find fences made of rows of trees.
Simple wooden houses are very common in South East Sulawesi. These houses often have tiled roofs, vertical wooden window bars and open roof sections.
In the Sornako area of Luwu Timor Regency, you can see many prefabricated houses, often on stilts.

Toli-Toli Regency also has a higher density of Bugis-style stilt houses than any other part of Central Sulawesi. A defining characteristic of Toli-Toli Regency is the colour blue. You will see blue utility poles, signs, entrance gates, and even the Sula fences are mostly painted blue and white.

A Tongkonan is the traditional ancestral house of the Toraja people in South Sulawesi in Rante Pao and surrounding areas, easily recognized by its distinctive, boat-shaped saddleback roof pointing dramatically towards the sky.
Belitung Island, on the other hand, mainly has sheet metal roofs, which can be either a fresh silver colour or show signs of rust.
Black walls with light-coloured rocks are common on Kundur Island and Karimunbesar Island.
Block shaped multi-story houses featuring shops or garages on the ground floor are frequently found in urban areas of North Sumatra and Riau.
In addition to the palm-wood houses, there are also the well-known traditional Batak boat-shaped houses in the Lake Toba area. Most of the houses have highly recognisable criss-crossed stilts.
The vast majority of the population of Nias Island are adherents of Protestant Christianity. Churches are common and graves on private property are not unusual.

In the Riau Islands as well as in Northern Sumatra, houses often feature circular or semi-circular vents and windows with “spokes” radiating out from the centre . These are typically featured on the gable or above doors and windows. Similar windows and vents can be found elsewhere in Sumatra.
In Jambi, Riau and also Batam and Bintan, intertwining floral patterns on house gables are common.
In Bengkulu, you will rarely find isolated pillars with a floral motif on top at property entrances.
Property entrances in Lampung also frequently feature rectangular stone pillars, often decorated, and a concrete kerb.

cards.a: Sumatra - Gate Pillars South Sumatra & Jambi
cards.note: Entrance pillars can be found In South Sumatra and Jambi, usually taking a turret shape with a rising balustrade attached.
In Jambi, you'll commonly find pointy saddle roofs, consisting of a steep top part and a more shallow flap. These often have simple X-shaped or hook-shaped gable horns attached.
In the regions of Sumatra and Kalimantan that lie opposite Malaysia, many buildings have metal canopies with curved ends. These canopies are often blue or red.

Bargeboards consisting of a carved wooden frieze can be found throughout Bengkulu. This type of roof decoration can also be found in other parts of Indonesia, in particular in West Kalimantan and South Kalimantan.

In exceptional cases, this meta is also found in regions other than those previously mentioned.
New residential areas with rows of modern houses and paved with hexagonal paving stones are common on Karimunbesar Island.

The Batak Karo people in the north of North Sumatra province often construct houses with unique, highly ornate crowns, consisting of four-way gables topped off with buffalo head finials. Both modern and traditional varieties of this design exist.

Historic migration from Java has left a mark on architecture in Lampung.

Traditional Javanese tiles are common here, however the population density in Lampung is much lower, resulting in larger plots of land and widely spaced houses.

Lampung roofs often have tiles of different shades, from light orange to dark brown. There are also more houses built of wood in Lampung.
Limas houses are found in a narrow area in the Musi Banyuasin Regency. A characteristic feature of this house type is a top section that gradually descends forming a long street-facing extension.

Conspicuously long bamboo fences, usually laid horizontally, are commonly used to demarcate properties within villages in Bengkulu, and are also frequently found in rural areas. Vertically oriented bamboo fences are also common.

In addition loose piles of stones are common too. Combined with the moss gardens and long bamboo fences this can be a good indication of the province.
In coastal areas of north-east Sumatra (mainly Riau and Jambi), you can find low-stilt houses. In the north they are usually elevated by concrete frustums while wooden stilts are found further south.

In Mandailing Natal Regency, you will find houses with ornate gables and strikingly long gabled horns on large roofs. These are called Bagas Godang Panyabungan Tonga and are associated with the Batak Mandailing people.
In Bengkulu, houses often have clean corrugated metal gables, often coloured crimson or blue.
Aceh is a uniquely autonomous province and the only one where Sharia Law is officially applied. Mosques are, therefore, more common, large and ornate in this region than other parts of Indonesia.

Gables in Bengkulu are also frequently multi-layered, with notches or semi-circle patterns in the top layer. Similar notches specifically can rarely occur in other regions such as North Kalimantan and West Sulawesi.

The Omo Sebua Chief’s House, built on pillars with towering thatched roofs (or sheet metal roofs in modern versions), is characteristic of Nias Island. It is particularly common in the southern half of the island.

Everyday houses with roofs that curve outwards to the side can be found as detached houses or in rows of houses in the southern half of Nias Island. The roof shape is a partial imitation of the Chief's House.
On Nias Island, you will commonly find houses that have windows in the gable end with wooden shutters that swing open.
In the northern half of Nias Island, chieftain houses found have roofs with a significantly more rounded shape.

Another widespread type of house on Nias Island is simple houses built from wooden planks and equipped with thatched roofs and thatched canopies over the front. The same combination of thatched roofs and canopies can also be found on other islands in Indonesia, but usually in different shapes.
The area south of Palembang is full of swamps. Stilt houses with hip metal roofs are common here.

Red bricks are very common in Sumatra and are helpful in regionguessing or excluding specific parts of the island. They occur in two variants: narrow and wide.

Narrow red bricks are found in the northern and southern parts of Sumatra, as well as all along the west coast.

Red bricks are very common in Sumatra and are helpful in regionguessing or excluding specific parts of the island. They occur in two variants: narrow and wide.

Wide red bricks are found in the centre-south, primarily in South Sumatra and Jambi.
Low walls made of these dark red stones can be found along property borders, mostly in the south of Bintan Island, as well as very rarely on Batam Island.
Roofs similar to those found in Bangka Island are very common in the Riau Islands. These roofs typically consist of fibre cement sheets with grey tiles lining the edges.
Red tiles along the edges of fibre cement roofs make houses on Bangka Island easily recognisable. Fully tiled roofs are also common.

Smaller structures in North Sumatra will often feature a variation of the gable design with a jagged boat roof, as opposed to the smoother curve. The rising section can be found on one or both ends of the roof.
The Siger crown is a symbol of Lampung. Its design features a curved shape with seven or nine peaks. It can be found on gates, lamps, bridge stones, street signs and in other places.
In West Sumatra, you will often find houses with a boat-shaped roof—frequently multi-tiered—featuring soaring spires at the gable ends, giving them a majestic appearance.
Stone lamps are common at entrances in Lampung as well as in adjacent parts of South Sumatra.
South Sumatra houses with sheet metal roofs (often with a dark rust-brown tone) are found in the interior, mountainous parts of the province, and can be found also in western Jambi.

South Sumatra has very unique houses which typically consist of a top floor with many windows, serving as the main floor, built on top of a lower section which may sometimes just consist of stilts or pillars. A staircase leads to the top section. The whole house is built of timber.

Combined with a hip roof made of traditional tiles, this type of house is very recognisable.
